summary: HazeGuard is an advanced, sensor-neutral geospatial data pipeline and burning activity calendar that resolves the 26-year observational discontinuity between MODIS and VIIRS satellite active fire records. By implementing a rigorous 4-stage harmonization pipeline; incorporating global equal-area grid projection, automated industrial noise filtering, sensor-neutral time-gap activity scoring, and MODIS orbital drift correction, HazeGuard is able to transform raw, inconsistent satellite streams into reliable fire data for emergency responders and climate scientists.
details:
HazeGuard is a sensor-neutral, activity-state-model-based wildfire activity and monitoring pipeline designed to harmonize and analyze multi-year satellite fire detection datasets (MODIS and VIIRS).

The Challenge

Tracking multi-decade wildfire trends and agricultural burning patterns is crucial for disaster mitigation, carbon accounting, and atmospheric modeling. However, analysts face a major systemic barrier: transitioning from the MODIS sensor (~1 km spatial resolution, active since 2000) to the VIIRS sensor (~375 m spatial resolution, active since 2012) creates an artificial "explosion" in fire counts. Furthermore, aging satellite orbits (like Terra and Aqua) suffer from orbital drift, shifting local overpass times over decades and skewing historical time series. Without multi-stage harmonization, historical baselines are heavily distorted.

How does it work?

Our project uses a Python script that processes MODIS and VIIRS csv data into a harmonized fire timeline. It uses an activity state model where each fire detected is awarded a point proportional to the area that it covers on an equal area grid and the time between detections. This means that a detection from VIIRS near a MODIS detection would be awarded less points. The activity of grid cells is then exported as a CSV file that is used by the web app. The project also accounts for MODIS and VIIRS satellite drift.

The 4-Stage Harmonization Pipeline

Stage 1: Spatial Standardization (Proportional Splitting): All spatial detections are mapped onto a global equal-area grid (1000km^2). Using explode_to_cells, pixel footprints are proportionally split across boundaries so that varying sensor sizes never bias density counts.

Stage 2: Automated Noise Suppression (repeatFilter.py): Raw thermal data is saturated with permanent anomalies like industrial gas flares and volcanoes. The temporal persistence filter automatically detects and drops cells triggering high observation frequencies (>25 detections across three 30-day windows).

Stage 3: Sensor-Neutral Time-Gap Scoring (timeGapActivity.py): Unifying MODIS and VIIRS into a single temporal stream, the pipeline measures time intervals (t= 3.0 hours) since a cell was last observed. By enforcing a per-pass cap (pass_mode="cap"), high-resolution sensors with denser pixel counts cannot artificially inflate scores.

Stage 4: MODIS Orbital Drift Correction (correct_modis_drift): To neutralize decades of orbital decay on Terra and Aqua, the pipeline calculates exact local solar time (LST) deviations from nominal overpass hours (10:30/13:30 LST) and shifts timestamps back, ensuring true temporal alignment.

Validation & Output Deliverables

We validated our pipeline on 2018 active fire data across Indonesia (activity_daily.csv), successfully isolating seasonal agricultural clearing peaks and peatland smoldering events while stripping out static industrial infrastructure noise and orbital drift artifacts.

Benefits

HazeGuard allows old MODIS data to be used along with VIIRS data to help people such as data analysts, firefighters, etc. This preserves the current archive of MODIS data that could have been obsolete. This project also corrects the offset caused by the discontinuation of repairs on the MODIS satellites Aqua and Terra. Our project also isolates detections from man-made objects and true environmental events.

What we hope to achieve

We hope that our project can give valuable insights to firefighters, climate scientists, data analysts and other relevant parties to help them in the future by utilizing the extensive archive of MODIS data and the precision of VIIRS to conduct their projects with considerable ease.

NASA Data & Space Agency Resources Used

NASA Earthdata FIRMS: Near-real-time and historical archive active fire data ingestion.

MODIS Collection 6.1 (Terra & Aqua): Two-decade historical baseline (2000–present) with orbital drift correction.

VIIRS 375m (Suomi-NPP, NOAA-20/21): High-resolution modern satellite continuity.


What tools did we use?

The project was built with Python and Visual Studio Code for the back-end. The front-end was developed using Google Studio
